segments.text: If you watch this video until the end,
you'll learn everything you need to know
about one of the most important parts of
API design, pageionation, and we'll
fully understand this crucial feature by
building a hands-on example with Python.
Pageionation is a simple but very
powerful concept. Instead of returning
all the data at once, which can be huge
and inefficient, we return data in small
pieces, page by page. This makes our
applications faster, easier to use, and
much more scalable. Before we jump into
the project, there are a couple of
Python modules we need to install. You
can do that with pip. The commands are
simple. I've already installed them
before, so I won't run the command here,
but you should make sure those packages
are available in your environment. Now,
let's look at the code. We start by
importing fast API and uicorn. Then we
create an instance of fast API. I've
also prepared a fake data set of 100
products. Each product has an ID, a
name, and a price just to simulate what
a real database might look like. The
first pageionation style we'll implement
is limit and offset. The idea is very
straightforward. Limit tells the API how
many items you want, and offset tells
the API how many items to skip before
starting. You can see that limit and
offset together give you complete
control over which slice of the data set
you're receiving. Of course, the
downside is that with very large data
sets, using a huge offset can get
inefficient because the database still
has to skip over all those rows. The
second style we'll implement is
cursorbased pageionation. Here, instead
of skipping rows, we pass a cursor,
which is usually the last ID we saw. The
API then returns items after that ID.
This approach is usually faster and more
stable, especially when new records are
being inserted into the data set. Some
of the code might not have been
completely clear so far, but we'll test
all the possibilities using Postman in a
moment, and that's when it will really
make sense.
Once we have the code ready, we can run
the server with the command uvicorn main
app-re.
That starts our API at localhostport
8000. Now, let's move to Postman and
actually test it. First, let's try the
limit and offset endpoint. I set limit
equal to five and offset equal to zero.
I get the first five items, ids 1
through 5.
If I set offset to five, I get items 6
through 10.
If I set offset to 10, I get items 11
through 15. That's exactly how
pageionation should behave.
Now I test with just the limit. If I if
I set limit equal to five, I get items 1
through 5.
If I set it to seven, I get items 1
through 7.
Now, let's test the products cursor
endpoint with the limit and cursor
options. First, I set both limit and
cursor to five and I receive the data
from 6 to 10. The response also tells me
that the next cursor value is 10. If I
set the cursor to 10, then the items
from 11 to 15 will be fetched.
And if I set the limit to 10 while the
cursor is 10, I'll get items from 11 all
the way to 20. You can experiment with
different combinations of limit and
cursor to understand this behavior even
better. And that wraps up our session.
